questions.stem: Which of the following best defines supply-side policy?
options: Measures to raise productive capacity by improving incentives, skills, competition and infrastructure
Changes in government spending and taxation to influence demand
Changes in interest rates to influence borrowing
Regulations restricting prices and wages
questions.why: It is the only instrument that raises capacity, and the slowest to work.
whyNot: That is fiscal policy.
That is monetary policy.
Those are direct controls.

questions.stem: Which of the following best defines quantitative easing?
options: Central bank purchases of assets, financed by creating money, to lower long-term interest rates
A reduction in government spending to lower the deficit
A tax cut aimed at raising consumption
The sale of government bonds to reduce the money supply
questions.why: It was used once interest rates could go no lower, and it tends to depreciate the currency as a side effect.
whyNot: That is fiscal consolidation.
That is fiscal policy.
That is the opposite operation.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a direct control?
options: A price cap on essential goods
A cut in interest rates
An increase in income tax
Investment in training
questions.why: Capital controls and import restrictions are the other examples: they restrict behaviour directly rather than through prices or demand.
whyNot: That is monetary policy.
That is fiscal policy.
That is supply-side policy.

questions.stem: Which of the following best defines policy conflict?
options: A situation in which pursuing one macroeconomic objective worsens another
A disagreement between the government and the central bank
A situation in which two policies use the same instrument
A conflict between national and international policy
questions.why: Naming the conflict is the most reliable evaluation point in any policy question.
whyNot: That is an institutional disagreement.
That is an instrument clash rather than an objective conflict.
That is policy spillover.

questions.stem: Why is raising interest rates an inappropriate response to cost-push inflation from an oil price shock?
options: It reduces output and employment without addressing the cause, which the central bank cannot influence
It has no effect on aggregate demand
It raises import prices further
It is prohibited during a supply shock
questions.why: Diagnosing whether inflation is demand-pull or cost-push should come before any recommendation.
whyNot: It does reduce AD, which is the problem here.
Higher rates appreciate the currency, lowering import prices.
It is permitted, and it is simply poorly matched to the cause.

questions.stem: Which instrument reduces inflation without reducing output?
options: Supply-side policy, by raising productivity and shifting AS right
Monetary tightening, by raising interest rates
Fiscal tightening, by raising taxes
Price controls, by capping prices
questions.why: All the demand-side instruments reduce inflation by reducing demand and therefore output.
whyNot: That reduces AD and therefore output.
That reduces AD and therefore output.
They suppress measured inflation and create shortages.

questions.stem: Why is a floating exchange rate an advantage in responding to an external shock?
options: The currency adjusts automatically rather than the domestic economy having to
It prevents shocks from occurring
It fixes import prices
It removes the need for reserves and for any policy at all
questions.why: This is the strongest single argument for a floating rate.
whyNot: It cannot prevent external shocks.
It allows import prices to change.
It removes the need for reserves and not for policy.

questions.stem: Why is there no demand-side answer to a negative supply shock?
options: It raises the price level and reduces output at once, so any demand response worsens one to improve the other
Demand-side policy is prohibited during supply shocks
Supply shocks have no effect on demand
Supply shocks reverse themselves automatically
questions.why: Saying so is the correct answer rather than a failure to answer.
whyNot: It is permitted and simply cannot fix both.
They affect prices and therefore real incomes and demand.
They can persist for years.

questions.stem: Which of the following was part of the demand-side response to the 2008 crisis?
options: Coordinated fiscal stimulus, interest rate cuts to near zero, and quantitative easing
Tariff increases and import quotas across major economies
Immediate fiscal austerity in all major economies
A return to fixed exchange rates
questions.why: Bank recapitalisation and guarantees were also essential, as a precondition for any other policy working.
whyNot: Protection was largely avoided at that stage.
Austerity came later, after deficits had risen.
Major currencies continued to float.

questions.stem: What is the most commonly cited criticism of the 2008 demand-side response?
options: Deficits and debts rose sharply and QE raised asset prices and therefore wealth inequality
It failed to prevent the banking system from collapsing
Unemployment rose more than in the 1930s
It caused hyperinflation in the major economies
questions.why: Near-zero rates also persisted for a decade, leaving little room to respond to the next shock.
whyNot: The banking system was stabilised.
Unemployment rose by much less than in the 1930s.
Inflation remained low for years afterwards.

questions.stem: What is the lasting lesson of the 2008 policy response?
options: Demand-side policy can stop a collapse in demand and cannot repair a damaged supply side
Demand-side policy is always ineffective
Supply-side policy works faster than demand-side policy
Financial crises have no lasting effects
questions.why: That is why the recovery in output and productivity was slow even after demand had been restored.
whyNot: It prevented a far deeper depression.
Supply-side policy is much slower.
The effects on productivity and real wages persisted for years.

questions.stem: Why is the arm's length principle hard to apply to transfer pricing?
options: No comparable market price exists for intellectual property, brands and specialised components
Companies are not required to price intra-group transactions
Tax authorities cannot access company accounts
Arm's length pricing is prohibited by the WTO
questions.why: That is precisely where profit shifting is concentrated, which is why transparency and a minimum rate work better than case-by-case pricing rules.
whyNot: They must, and the question is at what price.
Authorities can access accounts, with limited capacity to audit them.
It is the internationally recommended standard.

questions.stem: Why does controlling TNCs require international rather than unilateral action?
options: Any country tightening alone risks losing the investment, which is a collective action problem
National governments have no legal authority over firms in their territory
International bodies collect all corporate taxes
TNCs are exempt from all national law
questions.why: Transparency and a minimum effective rate address the cause, which is the interaction of national systems.
whyNot: They do have authority within their territory.
Taxes are collected nationally.
They are subject to the law of each country they operate in.

questions.stem: Which measure directly attacks the benefit of shifting reported profit?
options: An international minimum effective corporate tax rate
A cut in the domestic corporation tax rate
A tariff on imported goods
A rise in the domestic VAT rate
questions.why: Country-by-country reporting is the complementary transparency measure.
whyNot: That is tax competition, which is the problem rather than the remedy.
Tariffs concern trade, not profit reporting.
VAT is levied on domestic spending.

questions.stem: Why can a policy that raises wealth inequality be described as an unintended consequence?
options: QE supported demand as intended and raised asset prices, benefiting existing wealth owners
The effect was the stated objective of the policy
Wealth inequality cannot be measured
QE had no effect on asset prices
questions.why: Unintended consequences are a standard feature of the risks and uncertainties facing policymakers.
whyNot: The objective was to support demand and the financial system.
It is measured, though less well than income inequality.
Asset price support was one of its mechanisms.

questions.stem: What is the best single sentence for evaluating any policy recommendation?
options: Policy is set using estimates of unobservable quantities derived from data that will later be revised
Policy always works exactly as intended
Policy effects can be predicted precisely
Policy has no effect on the economy
questions.why: The output gap, trend growth and the revenue-maximising tax rate cannot be observed at all.
whyNot: Behavioural responses and lags make outcomes uncertain.
Multipliers and elasticities vary with circumstances.
Policy effects are substantial.

questions.stem: What is the constructive conclusion about policymaking under uncertainty?
options: Build in flexibility and resilience rather than attempting precision
Abandon macroeconomic policy altogether
Rely entirely on discretionary intervention
Fix all policy settings permanently
questions.why: Automatic stabilisers, reserves, a diversified economy and fiscal space all reduce vulnerability without requiring correct forecasts.
whyNot: Policy prevented a far worse outcome in 2008.
Discretion suffers from lags and uncertainty.
Fixed settings cannot respond to shocks.
